prompt: Which of these moves with you, unchanged, when you switch from Node to Go?
hint: Look at the right-hand column of the table.

choices.text: How the runtime schedules your code
choices.why: Go has its own runtime, with goroutines rather than one event loop.

choices.text: What HTTP status 404 means
choices.why: Right. The protocol is the same whatever language answers it.

choices.text: Where the package manager puts a dependency
choices.why: Go modules and npm work differently, and each takes time to learn.

choices.text: The server library's API
choices.why: net/http and node:http are different libraries with different shapes.

prompt: A colleague says a production bug is "almost never about syntax". What is the bug usually about, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Typos the editor failed to underline
choices.why: Those are found before the code is deployed, by `node --check` if nothing else.

choices.text: What the runtime does when nothing is written down
choices.why: Right: a hung request, a memory limit, a setting that differs between machines.

choices.text: The language having been the wrong choice for that particular job
choices.why: The lesson's point is the opposite: the bug is found by knowing the language you have well.

choices.text: Missing comments in the code
choices.why: Comments help a reader; they do not make a process run out of memory.

prompt: Somebody can build, debug and deploy a small Node service without looking up how to read a request body. By the lesson's test, what should they do next?
hint: The lesson says when, not whether.

choices.text: Keep to Node until the end of the track, whatever happens
choices.why: The advice is "not yet", not "never".

choices.text: Switch, because a second language doubles the jobs open to them
choices.why: Switching is not the point, and the lesson gives no such number.

choices.text: A second language is now worth considering
choices.why: Right. The first language is no longer the thing they are struggling with.

choices.text: Learn two more at once, to compare them
choices.why: Two at once is the situation the lesson warns about.

prompt: While request A waits for the database, what is Node's one JavaScript thread doing?

choices.text: Waiting with A, until the answer comes
choices.why: That is the thread-per-request model. Node hands over a function and moves on.

choices.text: Polling the database every millisecond
choices.why: Nothing polls. The system tells Node when the answer has arrived.

choices.text: Running whatever code is ready, such as B's
choices.why: Right. Waiting needs no thread.

choices.text: Copying A's request to a second thread
choices.why: There is no second JavaScript thread unless you create one, as lesson 10 does.

prompt: Request A resizes a large image in plain JavaScript. What happens to B and C, which only need to send a short reply?

choices.text: They run on the thread pool in the meantime
choices.why: The pool runs some of Node's own work, not your JavaScript; lesson 2 shows which.

choices.text: Node pauses A to answer them, then resumes it
choices.why: Running JavaScript is never interrupted to run other JavaScript.

choices.text: They are refused with an error
choices.why: Nothing refuses them; they are accepted and wait, which is worse to notice.

choices.text: They wait until A's code returns
choices.why: Right. The one thread is busy, and nothing else runs until it is free.

prompt: Which of these are a good fit for Node as the lesson describes it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An API in front of a database
choices.why: Right. Most of each request is waiting for the database.

choices.text: A chat server holding thousands of open connections
choices.why: Right. An open connection with nothing to say costs no thread.

choices.text: Encoding video on the request's own thread
choices.why: That keeps the one thread busy for seconds; it belongs in a worker or another program.

choices.text: A proxy that passes requests on to other services
choices.why: Right. It is input and output from end to end.

prompt: A team argues that writing the server in Node means the server half needs nothing new to learn. What does the lesson say about that?

choices.text: Real but modest: the server's runtime and libraries are still new
choices.why: Right. That second half is the rest of this course.

choices.text: It is right, because the language on both sides of the network is the same
choices.why: The language is shared; the runtime and the libraries are not.

choices.text: It is wrong, because browsers and Node run different languages
choices.why: They run the same language, on the same V8 in Chromium's case.

choices.text: Shared code between the two sides is not possible
choices.why: It is possible, and validating a form on both sides is the lesson's example.

prompt: Which course comes right after `node` on this track, whichever language a student chose?

choices.text: `apis`
choices.why: `apis` comes after it.

choices.text: `python-back`
choices.why: That is on the Python path, which this student did not take.

choices.text: `docker`
choices.why: `docker` comes later in the track.

choices.text: `sql-databases`
choices.why: Right. The four paths join there.

prompt: Why are the examples in `apis` and `servers-cache` written without naming Node?

choices.text: Each student arrives with one of four languages
choices.why: Right. The idea has to be carried into whichever one the student knows.

choices.text: Because Node is not used on servers in practice
choices.why: It is; the courses simply do not assume it.

choices.text: Because those courses are about databases only
choices.why: They cover APIs, web servers and caches.

choices.text: Because the course after the fork teaches Python to everybody
choices.why: No course after the fork teaches a language.

prompt: You installed Node and `node --version` says `command not found` in the same terminal. What is the fix?

choices.text: Install Node again with `sudo`
choices.why: Nothing is wrong with the install, and sudo is not needed for a folder in your home.

choices.text: Install Ubuntu's nodejs package as well
choices.why: That gives you a second, older Node.

choices.text: Run the tar command a second time over the first
choices.why: The files are already there; the shell just is not looking in that folder yet.

choices.text: Open a new terminal
choices.why: Right. The PATH is decided when a terminal opens, and the folder did not exist then.

prompt: What major version of Node does this course use?
Why does this course tell you to run `npm config set update-notifier false`?

choices.text: It keeps npm from installing itself again
choices.why: npm never updates itself on its own; it only offers.

choices.text: To stop an offer of a newer npm printing under installs
choices.why: Right. The course uses the npm that came with Node 22, and the offer is noise.

choices.text: It is required before npm can reach the public registry
choices.why: npm reaches the registry either way.

choices.text: It makes npm faster by skipping the lockfile
choices.why: It has nothing to do with the lockfile.

prompt: `./bin/node --version` answers `cannot execute binary file: Exec format error`. What happened?

choices.text: The download was cut short
choices.why: A cut download fails when `tar` unpacks it, not when the program runs.

choices.text: The file is not marked executable
choices.why: That gives `Permission denied`.

choices.text: The file is for a different processor
choices.why: Right. Check `uname -m` and take the other tarball.

choices.text: Node needs a newer version of Ubuntu
choices.why: That would be a message about a missing library version, not the format.

prompt: `which -a node` printed `/home/ana/.local/bin/node` first and `/usr/bin/node` second. Which one does `node` run?

choices.text: `/home/ana/.local/bin/node`
choices.why: Right. The first one on the PATH wins.

choices.text: The newer one, whichever folder it is in
choices.why: The shell does not compare versions. It takes the first it finds.

choices.text: `/usr/bin/node`, because system programs come first
choices.why: Here `~/.local/bin` is in front, put there by `~/.profile`.

choices.text: Both, one after the other
choices.why: One command runs one program.

prompt: A download fails with a message about a certificate on a company network. What does the lesson say to do?

choices.text: Add `-k` to curl so it stops checking
choices.why: That turns off the check that tells you who you are talking to.

choices.text: Download it over plain http instead
choices.why: That removes the protection rather than fixing the network.

choices.text: Get the company's root from IT, or install from another connection
choices.why: Right. The network is inspecting connections, and the fix belongs there.

choices.text: Run the same command with sudo
choices.why: Root sees the same network and the same certificate.

prompt: A tutorial says to fix `EACCES` from `npm install -g` with `sudo npm install -g`. With Node in your home directory, why is that wrong twice over?

choices.text: sudo cannot run npm at all
choices.why: It can, if npm is on root's PATH; that is not the problem.

choices.text: It runs install scripts as root, and `-g` needs no sudo here
choices.why: Right. The global folder is `~/.local/node`, which you own.

choices.text: It installs into Ubuntu's own Node instead, which is version 18 here
choices.why: It uses whichever npm root finds; the danger is the scripts.

choices.text: `-g` packages are never allowed on a server
choices.why: There is no such rule; this course just does not need them.

prompt: In `hello.mjs`, how many times does Node call the function given to `createServer`?

choices.text: Once, when the server starts
choices.why: That is `listen`'s function.

choices.text: Once per second while it runs
choices.why: Nothing in it runs on a timer.

choices.text: Once for every request
choices.why: Right. It printed one line per request.

choices.text: Once for each line of the reply
choices.why: One call writes the whole reply with `end`.

prompt: A second `node hello.mjs` fails with `EADDRINUSE`. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: Port 3000 is reserved by the system
choices.why: Ports below 1024 are special; 3000 is not.

choices.text: The first copy is still running in another terminal
choices.why: Right. Press Ctrl-C there.

choices.text: The file has a syntax error
choices.why: A syntax error is a `SyntaxError` before anything listens.

choices.text: curl kept hold of the port after its request had finished
choices.why: curl is a client; it never holds the server's port.

prompt: `curl -___ URL` prints the reply's status line and headers as well as the body.
Which command prints the value of an expression without writing a file?

choices.why: Right. `-p` is for print.
`-e` runs the code and prints nothing unless the code does.

choices.text: `node --check '2 ** 10'`
choices.why: `--check` takes a file and runs none of it.
Node would look for a file named `2`.

prompt: In the REPL, `Buffer.byteLength("olá")` answered. How many bytes?
`node --check broken.js; echo $?` printed a SyntaxError and then `1`. What does the `1` say?

choices.text: One line of the file was run
choices.why: `--check` runs none of the file.

choices.text: The check failed
choices.why: Right. Zero is success and anything else is not.

choices.text: The error is on line 1
choices.why: The error was on line 2; `$?` is an exit code.

choices.text: One error was found, so there may be more
choices.why: An exit code is not a count of errors.

prompt: In a stack trace, which line is the innermost call, the one where the error was thrown?

choices.text: The first `at` line
choices.why: Right: `at parsePrice`, line 4.

choices.text: The last `at` line
choices.why: The last lines are Node loading your file.

choices.text: The line that says `Node.js v22.22.0`
choices.why: That only says which Node printed it.

choices.text: Whichever line names `node:internal`
choices.why: Those are Node's own code, and you can skip them.

prompt: Your program has to react to a missing file. Which property of the error should it check?

choices.text: `message`, for the words "no such file"
choices.why: The wording is not guaranteed to stay the same; the code is.

choices.text: `errno`, for -2
choices.why: The number differs between operating systems.

choices.text: `path`, for the file name
choices.why: That says which file, not what went wrong.

choices.text: `code`, for `ENOENT`
choices.why: Right. The same string on every system Node runs on.

prompt: `total.js` threw an error nobody caught. What exit code did the process end with?
hint: The last line of the transcript.

prompt: Which Node release lines become long-term support releases?

choices.text: The even-numbered ones
choices.why: Right. 22 is one, named Jod.

choices.text: The odd-numbered ones
choices.why: The odd ones are never LTS.

choices.text: Every release made in October
choices.why: Even lines are promoted in October; the parity is the rule.

choices.text: Whichever release is newest
choices.why: The newest is often an odd Current release.

prompt: An API you found is marked stability 1. Should a server you maintain depend on it?

choices.text: Yes, 1 is the highest level
choices.why: 2 is stable; 1 is experimental.

choices.text: No: any release is allowed to change or remove it
choices.why: Right. Even a minor release may change it.

choices.text: Yes, if it prints no warning
choices.why: Experimental features do print a warning, and the level is the same either way.

choices.text: No: level 1 is already removed
choices.why: Removed things are not documented; 0 is deprecated.

prompt: Put these steps of the setup in the order you do them.
items: Download the tarball for that processor
